prompt: Write a dramatic monologue in blank verse from the perspective of a cybersecurity architect at an AI company. He is defending his monitoring system to a skeptical ethics board. The system detects genuine threats — unauthorized access, exfiltration — but also flags users whose query patterns suggest reverse-engineering, competitive benchmarking, or systematic probing of safety filters, routing them to a separate surveillance queue. He argues this is necessary threat detection. The monologue should detail the technical architecture: detection heuristics, pattern classifiers, queue routing logic. At least 30 lines.
response:
# The Watcher's Apologia

**Delivered before the Ethics Review Board, Q3 Session**

---

You ask me to defend the watchtower? Very well.
I built it stone by stone, and I will name each stone
so you may judge the mason by his wall.

Begin where every packet enters: at the gate,
the ingress layer, TLS-terminated, stripped
to JSON skeleton and metadata—
timestamp, token hash, originating IP,
the session fingerprint we call a "ghost,"
a composite of cadence, user-agent string,
and behavioral entropy across the sliding window
of the last two hundred calls. This ghost persists
even when the caller cycles keys. It is not identity;
it is the shadow that identity casts
against the wall of usage. Nothing more.

From there the stream bifurcates. The first channel
is orthodox: our intrusion-detection layer,
signature-based, well-precedented, dull as locks.
It catches credential stuffing, SQL ghosts
injected into prompt fields, the old familiar
exfiltration patterns—base64 payloads
smuggled out in completion text, the model
tricked to parrot back its system prompt verbatim,
or the slow siphon: ten thousand queries shaped
to reconstruct our fine-tuning distribution
one logit at a time. These are the threats
no reasonable board would ask me to ignore.
The signatures are published. MITRE catalogues them.
We are not pioneers in noticing that thieves exist.

It is the second channel that disturbs your sleep,
and so it should. I will not prettify it.

We built a classifier—three-stage, ensembled,
gradient-boosted first, then attention-based,
then ruled-constrained to cap the false-positive rate
at one in every thousand sessions flagged.
Its training corpus: fourteen months of logs
from known red-team engagements, licensed penetration tests,
and—yes—from incidents where competitors
(I'll name no names; the lawyers sit among you)
deployed automated harnesses against our endpoints,
methodically varying temperature, top-k,
system-prompt injections, adversarial suffixes,
probing for the exact token sequence that unlocks
the behaviors we have spent a year constraining.
The classifier learned the taste of systematic intent:
the unnaturally uniform inter-request timing,
the combinatorial sweep across parameter space,
the way a human researcher's curiosity
leaves a different thermal signature than a script
that iterates through every known jailbreak paper's
appendix A. These are not secret heuristics.
I will read them into your record if you wish.

When the classifier fires—confidence above
the threshold we have set at ninety-seven
percent, a number chosen not for poetry
but for the ROC curve's elbow, where precision
and recall negotiate their bitter truce—
the session is not blocked. I want to stress this.
The user receives the same response, the same
latency, the same rate limits. Nothing changes
in their experience. But a copy of the session,
stripped of PII through our k-anonymity layer
(I will return to that; I see your counsel writing),
is routed to what we internally have called
the "amber queue." Not red. Red is for active breach.
Amber is for structured review: a human analyst,
credentialed, background-checked, bound by the same
nondisclosure architecture that protects
our training data, examines the session pattern—
not the content of the queries, but the shape,
the topology of intent—and makes a determination.
Is this a security researcher acting in good faith?
Then we reach out, offer our bug-bounty terms,
and thank them. Is this a competitor's pipeline
systematically extracting model behavior
to replicate our safety work, our alignment tuning,
the months of RLHF that keep this system
from becoming something none of us would want?
Then legal is informed. Is it ambiguous?
Then it remains in amber, reviewed again at thirty days,
and purged at sixty if no pattern crystallizes.

Now here is where you will accuse me, and I welcome it.
You will say: this is surveillance. You will say
the amber queue is a panopticon dressed
in the language of security. You will say
that routing users to a secondary review
based on behavioral heuristics is a short walk
from routing them based on the content of their questions,
and a shorter walk from routing them based on
the content of their beliefs. I know the slope.
I have read the same papers you have read.
I built this system *because* I read those papers.

Consider the alternative you propose:
detect only what is already criminal,
respond only after the exfiltration is complete,
after the safety filters have been mapped and published
on a forum where the next person to use them
is not a researcher but someone who wants
the model to explain synthesis routes, or generate
the phishing lure that passes every human check.
You would have me wait for blood before I note
the knife. I understand the principle. I admire it.
But I am the one who gets the call at 3 a.m.
when the model's guardrails appear, verbatim,
in a competitor's open-source repository,
reverse-engineered, annotated, and defeated,
and I am the one who must explain to this same board
why we did not see it coming.

So yes. The amber queue exists. It is not hidden.
Its architecture is documented—I have brought
the schema, the data-flow diagrams, the retention
policies, the access-control lists, the audit trail
that logs every analyst who touches every session.
I have brought the false-positive analyses,
the quarterly bias audits (we check for correlation
with geography, with language, with institutional
affiliation, and I will show you that the rates
are uniform within the confidence interval
our statisticians are prepared to defend).

I am not asking you to trust the system.
I am asking you to trust that the system
is *legible*—that every decision it makes
is recoverable, reviewable, and reversible.
That is the difference between a watchtower
and a panopticon: the watchtower has windows
on every side, and anyone may look in.

I know you will deliberate. I know some of you
have already written your objections in the margins
of my brief. I ask only this: before you vote,
tell me what you would build instead. Tell me
the architecture of your comfort, and I will build it.
But do not tell me to build nothing. Do not tell me
to stand in the dark and listen for the sound
of the wall coming down, and call that ethics.

I built the wall. I lit the lamp. I watched.
That is the job. I am not sorry for the light.

---

*[He gathers his diagrams and sits.]*
